summary: A 1980 specification of the Telnet protocol, which gives remote text terminal access across the network. It was replaced by RFC 854.

plainLanguage.summary: Telnet lets you type at one computer and use another computer far away. This is an earlier version of the rules.

questions: what is a network virtual terminal
subtitle: A 1980 specification of Telnet: a virtual terminal, negotiated options and a handful of control commands.

tldr.problem: Hosts needed a standard way to connect terminals and terminal-oriented processes without knowing each other's terminal characteristics.
tldr.mechanism: Telnet runs over a TCP connection and rests on a Network Virtual Terminal, option negotiation with DO, DON'T, WILL and WON'T, and a symmetric view of both ends.
tldr.outcome: This specification was obsoleted by RFC 854.

facts.label: NVT character set
facts.value: Seven-bit USASCII in an eight-bit field

today: RFC 764 was obsoleted by RFC 854, which is the later Telnet protocol specification.

sections.title: Purpose and Core Ideas
sections.content:
Telnet provides a fairly general, bi-directional, eight-bit byte oriented communications facility. Its main goal is a standard method of interfacing terminal devices and terminal-oriented processes. A Telnet connection is a TCP connection carrying data with interspersed Telnet control information.

It is built on three ideas: the Network Virtual Terminal (NVT), negotiated options, and a symmetric view of terminals and processes.
sections.plainLanguage: Telnet is a shared language so any keyboard can talk to any faraway computer, as if everyone agreed to pretend they have the same kind of keyboard.

sections.title: Option Negotiation
sections.content:
Either party may request that an option take effect, and the other may accept or reject. A rejected option leaves the connection as an NVT. A party may refuse to enable an option but must never refuse to disable one. WILL offers to perform an option and DO requests it, with WON'T and DON'T as refusals.

To avoid endless acknowledgment loops, parties may only request a change of state, must not acknowledge a request to enter a mode they are already in, and rejected requests should not be repeated until something changes.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side asks "can we do it this way?" and the other says yes or no. You never keep asking after a no, or you would go in circles.

sections.title: The Network Virtual Terminal
sections.content:
The NVT is an imaginary bi-directional device with a printer and a keyboard, using seven-bit USASCII in an eight-bit field. By default it is treated as half-duplex and line-buffered, and a process that has finished sending and needs input must send Go Ahead (GA).

The sequence CR LF means new line, and CR NUL means a carriage return alone. Five control functions have standard representations: Interrupt Process (IP), Abort Output (AO), Are You There (AYT), Erase Character (EC) and Erase Line (EL). The Synch signal combines a TCP Urgent notification with the Data Mark (DM) command to clear the data path.
sections.plainLanguage: The NVT is a pretend standard keyboard and printer that everyone translates to and from, so nobody needs to know what the other person really has.

sections.title: Commands and Port
sections.content:
A command is the escape byte IAC (255) followed by a command code, and option commands add a third byte for the option. Examples: SE 240, NOP 241, Data Mark 242, Break 243, IP 244, AO 245, AYT 246, EC 247, EL 248, GA 249, SB 250, WILL 251, WON'T 252, DO 253, DON'T 254. Only IAC needs doubling to be sent as data.

For remote terminal access, the server listens on well known TCP port 23 (27 octal).
sections.plainLanguage: Special messages begin with a signal byte that says "this is a command, not text". The computer listens at door number 23.

items.label: Data Mark
items.desc: Data stream portion of a Synch; accompanied by TCP Urgent.

items.label: SB
items.desc: Subnegotiation of the indicated option follows.

items.label: WILL
items.desc: Desire to perform, or confirmation of performing, an option.

items.label: DO
items.desc: Request that the other party perform an option.

items.label: DON'T
items.desc: Demand that the other party stop an option.

items.label: IAC
items.desc: Data byte 255 when doubled; the command escape.
